Phoropter's first revisit. Written straight to plans/ without a draft in a cart, because how to do it was already agreed in sorrel's cart. The revisit's outcome: quince's ground holds except for the one decline, which is reversed. Nothing departed from this plan, so there's no Changed:.

One finding, worth having before an "open guesses" page exists: "no verdict" isn't "open". Before this as-built, five guesses had no verdict, and only burlap's own was really open (it's answered below). Gimlet's two and tamarind's one were answered in Changed: entries, before grommet gave answers a kind. Pumice's @source guess was answered by vellum, a different plan, two hops away through vellum's guess. A page of open guesses would have to say which it means, or it would list four answered guesses as open.

Chose: On a guess, the verdict sits in the sentence that links its answer

where src/render.ts file page

quote return `<p class="pair">Answered in ${entry.answeredBy.map((a) => `${link('answered-by', 'answeredBy', a, 'the as-built')}: ${verdictHtml(a.entry)}`).join(', ')}.</p>`;

Because (Claude, not asked): "Answered in the as-built: held." The verdict belongs to the answer, so on the guess it travels with the link to it rather than becoming a property of the guess itself. An agent finds it as verdict inside the guess's entry either way. Disproved and partly disproved are colored like a missing quote; held and not tested aren't colored at all.

Chose: An answer with no verdict still shows its link, with a note

where src/render.ts file page

quote : '<span class="note">no verdict (it doesn’t open with held, disproved, partly disproved, or not tested)</span>';

Because (Claude, not asked): the plan said it says so plainly. The note names the four words, so a writer who sees it knows what to change in the next as-built.

Answered: An answer's first word is the verdict its author meant

Answers the plan’s guess: held.

Answer (measured): held, on eight of eight. Every answer in mock-control and phoropter opens with a verdict (seven held, one disproved), and none of their prose contradicts it in a way that would mislead. Quince's "held on what exists, and not yet tested against what would disprove it" reads as held, which is what its author (Claude) meant: the guess held on every case that existed. That's one ambiguous case resolved the author's way, not a test of the rule against an answer written to mislead it.
